title: The Gates Shut at Curfew: Rousseau from the Grand-Rue to the Panthéon
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Geneva, Grand-Rue: the watchmaker's son is born
stops.date_confidence: attested; 28 June 1712 given by English Wikipedia and by the Confessions, Book I
stops.campa: In a house on the Grand-Rue, in the upper town of the Calvinist republic, Isaac Rousseau the watchmaker and Suzanne Bernard have a second son. Puerperal fever takes her within days. The child lives. Isaac keeps the boy and reads with him at night, the two of them working through Plutarch and the romances his wife left behind until the morning birds start. Geneva at this date is a city of some twenty thousand souls, sovereign, walled, and certain of itself. Its citizen is born owing it a name he will sign on his books for sixty years.
sources: Maison natale, Grand-Rue 40, Geneva, preserved as a museum
suggested_refs: The birth house at Grand-Rue 40, Geneva, now the Espace Rousseau

stops.name: Cathédrale Saint-Pierre, Geneva: the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested; Geneva parish baptismal register, cited at second hand through Cranston and Damrosch
stops.campa: Six days after the birth the child is carried up to the cathedral of Saint-Pierre, stripped of its images two centuries before and kept bare, and entered in the register of the Reformed church. The rite makes him a Genevan and a Calvinist at once, the two being one status in this city. He will trade both away at fifteen for a bed in Turin, buy them back at forty-two by public abjuration in this same building, and renounce them for good in 1763, in a letter, from exile.
sources: Geneva parish baptismal records as cited in standard Rousseau biographies (Cranston, Damrosch)
suggested_refs: The baptismal register of Saint-Pierre for July 1712

stops.name: Bossey: the broken comb
stops.date_confidence: attested for the residence 1722-1724 (English Wikipedia, 'Bossey'); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates disputed: 46.1667/6.15 and 46.1706/6.2394 also circulate, the latter about six kilometres east of the village
stops.campa: Isaac Rousseau flees the city after a quarrel he will not answer for in court, and the ten-year-old is boarded with his cousin Abraham Bernard at the house of the pastor Lambercier in Bossey, a Savoyard village under the Salève. Here a comb is found broken, the boy is accused, and he refuses to confess a thing he did not do. He is beaten for it twice. In the Confessions the episode runs for pages: the first injustice, and the end of childhood as he reckons childhood.
suggested_refs: The Lambercier parsonage at Bossey, Haute-Savoie

stops.name: Geneva: the engraver's workshop
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1725-1728; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Back in the city, apprenticed to the engraver Abel Ducommun, he learns the burin and the taste of a master's fist. He steals asparagus, apples, and tools; he lies about it; he reads whatever he can carry into the shop, and is beaten for reading. Three years of this teach him what the treatises will later argue at length: that a man kept in dependence learns deceit as a trade before he learns any other. He is not yet sixteen and he already hates the work of his hands.
suggested_refs: The workshop of Abel Ducommun in the Geneva old town

stops.name: Geneva: the gates shut at curfew
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources disagree on his age, the chronology lens and English Wikipedia saying fifteen and the geography lens saying sixteen. Born 28 June 1712, he was fifteen
stops.campa: On a Sunday evening in March he comes back late from walking outside the walls and finds the drawbridge up for the third time. A third late return means a beating he has already priced. He turns around at the gate. He is fifteen, he has no money, no trade he will admit to, and no plan beyond the Savoyard side of the border. He does not see Geneva again for twenty-six years, and when he does it is to stand before the consistory and ask for his citizenship back.
suggested_refs: The Geneva city gates and their curfew drawbridge, closed nightly against latecomers

stops.name: Annecy: Palm Sunday at the door of Madame de Warens
stops.date_confidence: attested; Confessions, Book II, and the Annecy municipal plaque at the Cour Saint-Maurice
stops.campa: A Catholic priest at Confignon feeds the runaway and sends him on with a letter to a convert baroness at Annecy. He expects a devout old crone; he finds Françoise-Louise de Warens, twenty-nine, separated from her husband, pensioned by the King of Sardinia to bring Protestants over. She reads the letter at her door on Palm Sunday and keeps him. She will be his patron, his teacher, his employer, and his lover, and he will call her Maman to the end of his life.
sources: Annecy municipal plaque at Cour Saint-Maurice
suggested_refs: The house of Mme de Warens at Annecy, Cour Saint-Maurice

stops.name: Turin: the hospice of the catechumens
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1728; day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: She sends him over the Alps to Turin, to the hospice where converts are lodged, instructed, and turned out with a little money. He spends some weeks among vagrants and professional abjurers, resists a fellow inmate who corners him, argues doctrine badly, and abjures. The paper costs him his Genevan citizenship, which is the only property he owns. He walks out with about twenty francs and the shame he will spend the second book of the Confessions itemising rather than excusing.
suggested_refs: The Hospice des Catéchumènes at Turin, receiving house for converts from the Protestant cantons

stops.name: Turin: Marion and the ribbon
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1728-1729; month and day unknown, defaulted to December 1728 to keep travel order
stops.campa: He takes service as a footman, first to Madame de Vercellis, at whose death he is present, then in the house of the Comte de Gouvon, where a place is being made for him. A pink and silver ribbon goes missing. Rousseau has taken it; he names the young cook Marion when questioned, and she is dismissed on his word and disappears. He confesses the theft forty years later in print, not to be absolved, and writes that the memory of her face has never once let him sleep easily.
suggested_refs: The Vercellis and Gouvon households of Turin, Rousseau's two years in service

stops.name: Annecy: the return over the mountains
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1729; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The chronology lens wrongly places the seminary at Turin in 1728
stops.campa: He walks back across the mountains to Annecy and to Mme de Warens, who takes him in, feeds him, and puts him into a seminary that gives up on him within months. She sets him to music instead: solfège, copying, the harpsichord, an education he assembles himself out of theory books and gets wrong for years before he gets it right. He teaches, he wanders as far as Lausanne and Neuchâtel and Paris, and he keeps coming back to her table the way a debt comes back.
suggested_refs: The Lazarist seminary at Annecy, which dismissed him as unteachable

stops.name: Chambéry: the land registry
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1731; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The claim that he became her lover around 1732 is tagged [R] in the research pool and rests on his own account
stops.campa: Mme de Warens moves her household down to Chambéry, capital of Savoy, and he follows into a clerk's stool at the royal land survey, registering plots for taxation. It lasts about a year. He gives it up for music lessons at a livre an hour to the daughters of Chambéry, and reads everything: Descartes, Locke, Voltaire, geometry, chemistry, botany, in no order and with no teacher. He is around twenty when he becomes her lover, on her initiative, and records that he felt more grief in it than joy.
suggested_refs: The Savoyard cadastral survey office at Chambéry, where he kept the register

stops.name: Les Charmettes: the happiest years
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia gives 1735-1736, the geography lens 1735-1738, French Wikipedia 1736-1742 with the summers of 1736 and 1737 and the winter of 1738-39. Defaulted to 1736-01-01; not resolved
stops.campa: Outside the town, in a valley under vines, Mme de Warens rents a house with a garden and an orchard. He rises before the sun, works his Latin and his algebra in the fields, dresses the beehives, walks, and believes himself dying of a heart complaint that will not kill him for another forty years. He writes later that here alone he was entirely himself and entirely happy, and that nothing afterwards was worth the trade. The house stands today as the Musée Jean-Jacques Rousseau.
suggested_refs: Les Charmettes, near Chambéry, preserved as the Musée Jean-Jacques Rousseau

stops.name: Lyon: tutor to the Mably children
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1740; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. He also lodged at Lyon in 1730-1731
stops.campa: He takes a post at Lyon in the house of Jean Bonnot de Mably, provost general of police, tutoring two small boys whose uncles are the abbé de Mably and the philosopher Condillac. He is a bad tutor, impatient and theoretical, and he knows it; the treatise on education that will make his name is written by a man who failed at the practice and never claims otherwise. He leaves after a year with a draft of a system of musical notation in his baggage.
suggested_refs: The Mably household at Lyon, Rousseau's one experiment in tutoring

stops.name: Paris: the notation by numbers
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1742; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He arrives with fifteen louis, a comedy, a system for writing music in numerals instead of staves, and letters to whoever will read them. The Académie des Sciences hears the system out, praises his industry, and rules it neither new nor useful. He publishes it himself and nobody adopts it. The drawing rooms open anyway: he plays chess at the Café de la Régence, dines with Diderot, who is his own age and equally poor, and becomes a familiar of the salon of Madame Dupin.
suggested_refs: Rousseau's Dissertation sur la musique moderne (1743), the rejected notation system in print

stops.name: Venice: the French embassy
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1743-1744; month uncertain, set to September 1743. Coordinates mark central Venice: the embassy building was not identified, and the gap is recorded
stops.campa: Secretary to the Comte de Montaigu, ambassador of France to the Republic, he does the ciphers, the dispatches, and the ambassador's thinking for about a year while Montaigu drinks. He learns what a state is by watching a decayed one work, and will write afterwards that everything holds at bottom to politics and that a people is whatever its institutions make of it. Then Montaigu throws him out of the house without his wages, and the embassy's immunity makes the injury unappealable.
suggested_refs: The French embassy at Venice under the Comte de Montaigu, 1743-1744

stops.name: Paris: Thérèse Levasseur and the Enfants-Trouvés
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1745; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01. The children were placed over subsequent years from about 1746
stops.campa: At a shabby table d'hôte on the rue Saint-Jacques he meets a laundry maid from Orléans, Thérèse Levasseur, barely literate, unable to read a clock. She stays with him thirty-three years. Five children are born to them and five are carried, each in turn, to the hospital of the Enfants-Trouvés, unregistered and untraceable, the last thread cut on purpose. The man who is about to teach Europe how to raise a child never sees any of his own again, and puts that in print himself.
suggested_refs: The Hôpital des Enfants-Trouvés, Paris, which by design kept no names

stops.name: Vincennes: the road to the prison
stops.date_confidence: attested for October 1749; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The chronology lens gives 48.8474/2.4387 for the same place
stops.campa: Diderot is locked in the keep at Vincennes for the Lettre sur les aveugles, and Rousseau walks the six miles out from Paris to visit him, reading the Mercure de France on the way to spare his eyes from the October sun. The Academy of Dijon asks whether the restoration of the sciences and the arts has purified morals. He sits down under a tree by the road and, by his own account, cannot get up again: he weeps for half an hour, soaks his waistcoat, and sees the whole of his philosophy at once.
suggested_refs: The road from Paris to the keep of Vincennes, walked in October 1749

stops.name: Dijon: the academy's prize
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia dates the prize 1750 and publication 1751, the Stanford Encyclopedia dates both to 1751. The chronology lens wrongly tags the award to Paris. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Académie des Sciences, Arts et Belles-Lettres de Dijon reads the anonymous entries and gives first prize to his. The Discourse argues that the arts and sciences have corrupted rather than purified, that Athens fell and Sparta stood, that politeness is a varnish laid over vice. It is printed and it detonates: refutations arrive from a king of Poland and from professors across Europe, and the copyist from Geneva is, at thirty-eight, the most argued-with man in France.
suggested_refs: The prize records of the Académie de Dijon for the 1750 concours

stops.name: Fontainebleau: Le Devin du village before the King
stops.date_confidence: attested for 18 October 1752 in the geography lens; the chronology lens gives only October 1752
stops.campa: His one-act pastoral opera is played before Louis XV at the château, and the King hums the airs off-key through the following morning. A pension is arranged; presentation to the King is arranged; and Rousseau, who has a weak bladder, a horror of ceremony, and a new doctrine that forbids him to be bought, absents himself and forfeits both. Diderot tells him he is a fool. The opera runs for decades and he never sees a fraction of the money it makes.
suggested_refs: Le Devin du village, first performed at Fontainebleau, October 1752

stops.name: Geneva: the reconversion
stops.date_confidence: attested for August 1754; day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He comes home a celebrity with the Discourse on Inequality half written and dedicated to the Republic of Geneva. The consistory receives him, he abjures the Roman church, and the citizenship he sold at fifteen in a Turin hospice is restored to him. From this point every title page carries the words: by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Citizen of Geneva. Eight years later the same city will burn two of his books, and he will write to the syndics giving the citizenship back.
suggested_refs: The Geneva consistory act of readmission, August 1754

stops.name: Paris: the Discourse on Inequality
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1755; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Dijon sets a second question, on the origin of inequality, and he answers it at a length no prize can accommodate and loses. The Discourse invents a man before society: solitary, mute, healthy, moved by pity, neither good nor wicked, and then shows property, metallurgy, and agriculture forging the chains link by link out of that innocence. Voltaire acknowledges his gift copy by writing that no one has ever used so much intelligence to turn us into beasts, and that reading it gives him an appetite to walk on all fours.
stops.quote: The first man, who, after enclosing a piece of ground, took it into his head to say, 'This is mine,' and found people simple enough to believe him, was the true founder of civil society.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality, Part Two, opening (Project Gutenberg ed. 11136)
sources: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (Project Gutenberg ed. 11136)
suggested_refs: Voltaire's letter of thanks for the gift copy, 30 August 1755

stops.name: L'Ermitage, Montmorency: Sophie d'Houdetot
stops.date_confidence: attested for the move to the Ermitage in 1756; the Houdetot attachment is dated 1757 by English Wikipedia (declaration 24 May 1757) against the chronology lens, which says 1756. Not resolved
stops.campa: Madame d'Épinay gives him a cottage on her estate in the valley below Montmorency, and he leaves Paris for good at forty-four, declaring that he will live by copying music and owe no man a dinner. Julie is begun here, out of a fever of imagined love, and then Sophie d'Houdetot rides up in men's clothes and the imagined thing acquires a face, a voice, and another man's claim on it. Grimm, Diderot, and Madame d'Épinay close on him at once. He leaves the Ermitage in December with the friendships broken.
suggested_refs: L'Ermitage on the d'Épinay estate at Montmorency, Rousseau's first country retreat

segments.name: Mont-Louis: Three Books in Four Years

stops.name: Mont-Louis, Montmorency: the house of the Luxembourgs
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1758-1762; month and day unknown, defaulted to June 1758
stops.campa: The Duc and the Duchesse de Luxembourg install him in a small house at Mont-Louis and then in a pavilion of their own château, feeding him, protecting him, and reading his manuscripts aloud in the evening. In four years at this address he finishes Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse, the Contrat social, and Émile. He copies music by the page the whole time to pay for his own bread, refuses the pensions offered him, and writes to his correspondents that he is dying and has little left to say.
suggested_refs: The house of Mont-Louis at Montmorency, preserved as the Musée Jean-Jacques Rousseau

stops.name: Paris: Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1761; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The novel in letters comes out at the start of the year and Paris cannot get copies. Booksellers rent it by the hour and by the day; women write to him about their tears; seventy editions appear before the century ends. It is the story of a tutor and his pupil who love each other, marry elsewhere, and build a household on renunciation instead of passion. The author is a man who left five infants at a hospital gate, and the readers who know that go on weeping anyway.
stops.quote: Virtue is a state of war, and to live in it means one always has some battle to wage against oneself.
stops.quote_source: Julie, ou la Nouvelle Héloïse (1761), Part VI, Letter VII, spoken by a character in the novel, not by Rousseau in his own voice; French verified via fr.wikisource
sources: fr.wikisource, Oeuvres completes de Jean-Jacques Rousseau, vol. II
suggested_refs: The Paris lending trade of 1761, which rented Julie out by the hour

stops.name: Amsterdam: Du contrat social off Rey's press
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1762; day unknown, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Marc-Michel Rey prints it in Amsterdam because no printer in France will touch it. It is short, it is cold, and it proposes that legitimate authority rests on nothing except the agreement of the governed and the general will they constitute between them. France bans its distribution, Geneva burns it, Rome puts it on the Index. It travels regardless. Simón Bolívar will read it in Caracas in his tutor's house, and Juana Azurduy and Manuel Padilla will court each other over borrowed copies in Charcas.
stops.quote: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.
stops.quote_source: The Social Contract, Book I, Ch. 1 (G.D.H. Cole translation, Project Gutenberg ed. 46333)
suggested_refs: The Marc-Michel Rey edition, Amsterdam 1762, first printing of Du contrat social

stops.name: Paris: Émile burned and the warrant issued
stops.date_confidence: attested; Émile published May 1762, the Parlement's condemnation and warrant dated 9 June 1762
stops.campa: Émile appears in May, and the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar inside it, which grants God and denies revelation, offends the Sorbonne, the Parlement, and the Archbishop at one stroke. On the ninth of June the Parlement orders the book torn and burned by the public hangman and issues a warrant for the author's arrest. The Prince de Conti sends word in the night and Rousseau is out of Montmorency by morning. In Königsberg, Immanuel Kant reads the same book and misses his afternoon walk.
stops.quote: God makes all things good; man meddles with them and they become evil.
stops.quote_source: Emile, or On Education, Book I opening line (Project Gutenberg ed. 5427, Foxley translation)
suggested_refs: The Parlement de Paris arrêt of 9 June 1762 condemning Émile

stops.name: Yverdon: the first refuge
stops.date_confidence: attested for 14 June 1762 by the geography lens; the chronology lens wrongly gives July 1762
stops.campa: He crosses into Bernese territory and stops at Yverdon with his old friend Roguin, a man of seventy who gives him a room and asks nothing for it. Geneva burns Émile and the Contrat social in the same weeks and issues its own warrant, so the republic he signs himself a citizen of has now joined France in wanting him arrested. Bern gives him about three weeks before ordering him out of the canton. He is fifty years old, and this is the start of five years of being moved along.
suggested_refs: The house of Daniel Roguin at Yverdon, first refuge of the exile

stops.name: Môtiers: the Armenian caftan
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1762-1765 residence; exact arrival day approximate. Coordinates disputed: 46.9333/6.7333 and 46.917/6.617 also circulate, the first about nine kilometres east of the Val-de-Travers
stops.campa: In the Val-de-Travers, in the Prussian principality of Neuchâtel, Lord Keith the governor gives him leave to settle, and Frederick the Great, whom he has insulted in print, declines to hold it against him. He wears a fur cap and a long Armenian caftan, which spares him the surgical business his bladder requires, and lets the village think what it likes. He botanises the Jura, writes the Lettres écrites de la montagne against Geneva, and is denounced from the pulpit for it.
suggested_refs: The Rousseau house at Môtiers, Val-de-Travers, under Lord Marischal's protection

stops.name: Môtiers: the stones against the house
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1765; the exact night is given variously and the day here is approximate
stops.campa: The pastor Montmollin preaches him out. The village, having tolerated the caftan and the visitors and the fame, turns; stones come through the windows at night, one of them large enough, he writes, to have killed him had it landed. He is fifty-three, he is under the protection of a king, and a country parish has evicted him with rocks. He leaves within days for an island in a lake, taking Thérèse, his plant press, and no clear idea where the next refusal will come from.
suggested_refs: The stoning of the Rousseau house at Môtiers, September 1765

stops.name: Île de Saint-Pierre, Lake Biel: the fifth walk
stops.date_confidence: attested for 10 September 1765. Coordinates disputed: 47.0964/7.0967 and 47.085/7.1667 both fall in open water off the island; the surveyed position is used here
stops.campa: A single house on a wooded island in the Lake of Biel, a steward's family, a boat, and about seven weeks. He unpacks nothing. He catalogues the island's plants, ferries rabbits across to a smaller island in a founding ceremony he conducts himself, lets the boat drift with his body lying in the bottom of it, and does no writing at all. In the Rêveries, at the end of his life, he calls this the only happiness he ever knew that asked nothing of the future.
sources: Rousseau, Reveries of the Solitary Walker, Fifth Walk
suggested_refs: St Peter's Island in the Lake of Biel, and the Fifth Walk of the Rêveries written about it

stops.name: Bern: the senate's order
stops.date_confidence: attested for 17 October 1765; he left the island on 29 October
stops.campa: The senate of Bern, which had already put him out of Yverdon, rules that the island is Bernese too and orders him off the canton's territory within a fortnight. He answers by asking to be imprisoned instead, for life, anywhere, on condition that he be left alone with his books. The request is refused as impertinent. He is on the road again by the end of October, with invitations in hand from Corsica, from Prussia, from Britain, and nowhere in Europe where he may simply live.
suggested_refs: The Bernese senate decree of 17 October 1765 expelling him from the canton

stops.name: Strasbourg: the winter of invitations
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay from late October to 9 December 1765; the geography lens gives the range as October to November, which ends it a month early
stops.campa: He lodges at Strasbourg for six weeks while the offers are weighed. The town turns out for him; the theatre plays Le Devin du village and the audience looks at his box rather than at the stage. Corsica wants a constitution written and he is tempted by it; Frederick offers Prussia; David Hume, from London, offers England, and keeps writing until his is the only offer still on the table. He accepts England. He sets out for Paris on the ninth of December, still under a French warrant of arrest.
sources: Rousseau's correspondence, 1765, as summarized in Cranston, The Solitary Self
suggested_refs: Rousseau's Strasbourg correspondence of November 1765, weighing Corsica, Prussia, and England

stops.name: Paris: the enclosure of the Temple
stops.date_confidence: attested for December 1765; the exact day of arrival is approximate
stops.campa: He crosses France to Paris openly, in the Armenian caftan, and lodges in the Temple, the Prince de Conti's enclosure, where the Paris police have no jurisdiction to follow him. The warrant of 1762 has never been lifted and the government elects not to see him. For a month the city files through his rooms: duchesses, philosophers, and the merely curious, who report that he is small, quick, courteous, and watching them. Then he takes the north road with Hume, who thinks he is bringing a friend home.
suggested_refs: The Temple enclosure in Paris, a jurisdiction outside the reach of the royal police

segments.name: England, and the Break with Hume

stops.name: London: arrival with David Hume
stops.date_confidence: attested for 13 January 1766; departure from Paris 4 January 1766
stops.campa: Hume brings him to London in January and finds him lodgings, a place at the theatre where the King and Queen look at him more than at Garrick, and a royal pension he has to be argued into accepting. Crowds want the caftan and the dog. Hume writes to his friends that he has never met a man of such gentleness and such feeling, and that he expects trouble from him; Rousseau writes that he cannot see the bottom of Hume's kindness, and begins, quietly, to look for it.
suggested_refs: The Hume-Rousseau correspondence of 1766, printed by both sides within the year

stops.name: Wootton Hall, Staffordshire: the Confessions begun
stops.date_confidence: attested for 22 March 1766. Coordinates disputed: 53.0333/-1.8667 and 53.0167/-1.8667 also circulate. The corpus holds no prior England pin for Rousseau, so nothing was inherited
stops.campa: Richard Davenport lends him a house in the Staffordshire hills, cold, remote, and surrounded by walking country. Thérèse comes over; they botanise the Weaver Hills; he begins the book about himself that nobody has attempted in this form. Then a satirical letter forged in Horace Walpole's hand circulates in Paris, and he concludes that Hume brought him to England in order to have him laughed at. The correspondence between them turns public and merciless. Hume prints it. He bolts from Wootton without notice.
stops.quote: I have entered upon a performance which is without example, whose accomplishment will have no imitator. I mean to present my fellow-mortals with a man in all the integrity of nature; and this man shall be myself.
stops.quote_source: The Confessions, Book I opening (Project Gutenberg ed. 3913)
suggested_refs: Wootton Hall, Staffordshire, where the first six books of the Confessions were drafted

stops.name: Dover: the embarkation for Calais
stops.date_confidence: contested: English Wikipedia and the chronology lens give 22 May 1767, the geography lens gives 21 May 1767. Not resolved
stops.campa: He and Thérèse take ship for Calais after sixteen months in England, leaving behind an unfinished manuscript, an unclaimed pension, and a quarrel that has been printed in two languages. He believes a conspiracy is arranged against him running through Hume, Grimm, Diderot, d'Holbach, and the ministries of two kingdoms. There is no such conspiracy, and there is no shortage of individual men who have in fact worked against him. He goes back to a country where his arrest is still lawful.
suggested_refs: The Dover packet to Calais, 22 May 1767, end of the English exile

segments.name: Renou: the Years Under a False Name

stops.name: Trie-Château: sheltered under the name Renou
stops.date_confidence: attested for June 1767 to June 1768 by French Wikipedia; day unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected from 49.3128/1.8306, which lies about three kilometres north of the village
stops.campa: The Prince de Conti, who warned him out of Montmorency in 1762, now hides him on an estate in the Vexin under the name Renou, with Thérèse passing as his sister. The authorities in Paris know exactly where he is and say nothing about it. He collects plants, copies music, writes at the second half of the Confessions, and reads the servants' whispers as evidence. He accuses the household of poisoning his wine and intercepting his letters, and after a year he leaves for the mountains of Dauphiné.
suggested_refs: The château of Trie in the Vexin, lent by the Prince de Conti to the fugitive Renou

stops.name: Bourgoin: the marriage to Thérèse
stops.date_confidence: attested for 30 August 1768; the municipal record is cited at second hand through Cranston
stops.campa: At an inn in Bourgoin, before two witnesses and an officer of the town, Jean-Joseph Renou takes Thérèse Levasseur to wife. The ceremony has no legal force and no clergy: a Protestant in France cannot marry, and Renou does not exist. He makes a speech about the union of hearts and both of them cry. They have been together twenty-three years, the five children are twenty years gone into the register of an institution that keeps no names, and neither of them ever speaks of retrieving them.
sources: Bourgoin municipal record as cited in Cranston
suggested_refs: The Bourgoin marriage of 30 August 1768, contracted under an alias and without legal standing

stops.name: Monquin, near Bourgoin: the farmhouse year
stops.date_confidence: attested for January 1769 to 10 April 1770; day of the move unknown, defaulted to 01. The geography lens tagged this stop [R]; the residence is attested and only the exact building is uncertain, so the coordinates are approximate
stops.campa: They move to an isolated farmhouse on a hillside above the Bourbre, rented cheap, and stay fifteen months. He is fifty-seven. He botanises the Dauphiné, dries specimens for correspondents, keeps a herbarium, and finishes the Confessions in a hand that never wavers even where the sense does. Thérèse is unhappy and says so. He writes long letters about the plot against him to people who have not written to him, and then he decides to go back to Paris and face it.
suggested_refs: The Monquin farmhouse near Bourgoin, in the commune of Maubec

stops.name: Paris, Rue Plâtrière: copying music by the page
stops.date_confidence: attested for 24 June 1770; he lived here until May 1778
stops.campa: He returns to the city that has a warrant out for him, takes a fourth-floor apartment on the rue Plâtrière with Thérèse, and posts a copyist's rate of ten sous the page. The police, again, decline to notice him. He reads the Confessions aloud in private houses in sittings of fifteen hours, until Madame d'Épinay asks the authorities to stop it and they do. That August, at Neuhof near Birr, Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi names his newborn son Jean-Jacques.
stops.quote: It is too difficult to think nobly when we think for a livelihood.
stops.quote_source: The Confessions, Book IX (Project Gutenberg ed. 3913); the widely quoted variant 'when one thinks only of earning a living' is not the text
suggested_refs: The rue Plâtrière, renamed rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau, and the fourth-floor copyist's rooms

stops.name: Paris: the Great Dane on the Ménilmontant road
stops.date_confidence: attested for 24 October 1776
stops.campa: On the road at Ménilmontant a nobleman's carriage comes through at speed behind a Great Dane, and the dog takes the sixty-four-year-old walker off his feet. He wakes on the cobbles bleeding from the mouth, his upper lip split and his thumb broken, and cannot say who he is or where he lives. Word goes round Paris that he is dead; one journal prints the notice and discusses the subscription for his monument. He reads his own obituary and takes it for further proof.
suggested_refs: The premature obituary of Rousseau printed in Paris in 1776

stops.name: Ermenonville: the Girardin park
stops.date_confidence: attested for 20 May 1778. Coordinates corrected: 49.1667/2.6833, 49.15/2.6733, and 49.1451/2.6772 all circulate and all fall two to four kilometres from the village
stops.campa: The Marquis de Girardin has spent a decade building a landscape garden out of the Nouvelle Héloïse, with a philosophers' grove and an inscription to Montaigne, and he offers its author a cottage inside it. Rousseau accepts, arrives on the twentieth of May with Thérèse, and spends six weeks botanising with the marquis's children, teaching them plants and songs. He is sixty-six, he has taken the Rêveries as far as the tenth walk, and he sleeps, his host says, without complaint.
suggested_refs: The park of Ermenonville, laid out by Girardin as a landscape reading of Julie

stops.name: Ermenonville: the second of July
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2 July 1778; cause given as cerebral haemorrhage
stops.campa: He walks at dawn as usual, takes coffee with Thérèse, and complains of cold in his feet and a violent pain rising through his head. He is dead before eleven. The cause given is a bleeding in the brain, and the wound on the forehead where he fell is enough to start a rumour of a pistol that will run for a hundred years; everyone who saw him in his last days describes a serene man. Houdon comes out from Paris the next day and takes the death mask in plaster.
suggested_refs: Houdon's death mask of Rousseau, ancestor of every later bust

stops.name: Île des Peupliers: the burial among the poplars
stops.date_confidence: attested for 4 July 1778. Coordinates from French Wikipedia; the geography lens gives 49.1494/2.6742, which falls outside the park
stops.campa: They bury him at night on a small island in the park lake, ringed with poplars, and the grave becomes a place of pilgrimage. Marie Antoinette comes out from Versailles to stand at it. Napoleon comes later and looks at the stone. Girardin keeps the setting as a scene out of the Nouvelle Héloïse, and the tomb is engraved, printed, and copied in gardens across Europe. Since the remains were taken to Paris the island has held an empty sarcophagus, a cenotaph in water.
sources: Girardin's park records; contemporary visitor accounts
suggested_refs: The empty mausoleum on the Île des Peupliers at Ermenonville

stops.name: Panthéon, Paris: laid a few paces from Voltaire
stops.date_confidence: attested for 11 October 1794; French Wikipedia's Île des Peupliers page says the tomb has been empty since 1793, which contradicts every other source and is recorded rather than corrected
stops.campa: Sixteen years after the burial the Convention has the coffin taken up, carried into Paris in procession with a bust and the Contrat social on a cushion, and laid in the Panthéon a few paces from Voltaire, who attacked him for twenty years and died six weeks before him. In 1821 both tombs are moved out of public view and stay inside the building. In 1952 Louis Braille is brought down into the same crypt, a village schoolmaster set among the writers who taught the Republic to argue.
suggested_refs: The Panthéon crypt, where Rousseau and Voltaire face each other across the aisle
